content: Loa loa is a filarial nematode, commonly referred to as the eye worm, that causes a condition known as Loa loa filariasis. This parasitic infection is primarily found in regions of Africa and India. Loa loa is one of three filarial nematodes that cause subcutaneous filariasis in humans, the other two being Mansonella streptocerca and Onchocerca volvulus (the latter being responsible for river blindness). The maturing larvae and adult worms of Loa loa inhabit the subcutaneous layer of human skin, also known as the fat layer, where they induce disease. The immature larvae develop within horseflies of the genus Chrysops (commonly known as deer flies or yellow flies), including species such as C. dimidiata and C. silacea. These flies transmit the infection to humans through their bites. Morphology Loa loa worms have a simple body structure consisting of a head, body, and tail. Male worms measure between 20 mm and 34 mm in length and 350 μm to 430 μm in width. Female worms are larger, ranging from 20 mm to 70 mm in length and approximately 425 μm in width. Life Cycle The life cycle of Loa loa involves three key species: the parasite itself, the fly vector, and the human host. When a vector fly bites an infected human, it ingests microfilariae (the larval stage of the parasite). The microfilariae migrate to the fat body of the insect host. Within the fly, the microfilariae develop sequentially into first-stage larvae, second-stage larvae, and finally third-stage larvae, which are infectious. The infectious third-stage larvae travel to the proboscis of the fly. When the infected fly bites an uninfected human, the third-stage larvae penetrate the skin and enter the subcutaneous tissue. The larvae mature into adult worms within the human host, where they produce microfilariae. These microfilariae can be found in the spinal fluid, urine, peripheral blood, and lungs. Pathogenesis Loa loa parasites infect humans by migrating through subcutaneous tissues, causing inflammation in the skin along their path. If a parasite remains stationary for a short period, it can trigger localized inflammation known as Calabar swellings. These swellings are tense, pruritic (itchy), inflammatory subcutaneous edemas that typically occur in the joints of the extremities, such as the wrists and ankles. They last for 1–3 days and represent areas of angioedema caused by the host's immune response to allergens released by the maturing worm and its metabolic byproducts. Calabar swellings resolve once the parasite resumes movement. The parasites can also migrate to and infect the eye, leading to swelling in the ocular region. Common symptoms of Loa loa infection include itching, joint pain, fatigue, and, in severe cases, death. Diagnosis and Treatment Diagnosis of Loa loa infection is based on the detection of microfilariae in the blood, the observation of a worm in the eye, or the presence of characteristic skin swellings. Surgical removal of the worm is a straightforward procedure. The primary pharmacological treatment for Loa loa filariasis is ivermectin, a widely used antiparasitic drug. However, ivermectin may leave behind residual microfilarial loads when used to manage loiasis. In cases of high microfilarial loads, the risk of severe adverse events, including fatal encephalopathy caused by dying microfilariae, necessitates reducing the load before treatment. This can be achieved through a course of ivermectin, prolonged administration of albendazole, or cytapheresis sessions. Cytapheresis is particularly effective, reducing microfilarial loads by up to 75%. Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is another treatment option that targets both microfilariae and adult worms. However, DEC is associated with more severe side effects and carries a risk of fatal outcomes.
